clue.text: Dodge pesticides heartlessly sprayed around

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letters of the word are cut out
something sprayed around is scattered in all directions, so its letters land in a new order

blocks.note: the word with its two middle letters, C and I, removed

explanation.surface: A farmer ducks out of the way as weedkiller is sprayed across the field.
explanation.walkthrough: PESTICIDES has ten letters, so its heart is the fifth and sixth, C and I; the eight left over rearrange into SIDESTEP.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidestep a blow or a question is to step aside and avoid it, a close synonym of dodging.

clue.text: Northbound motorway surrounded by river birds in season

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading north means reading from the bottom up
being surrounded means being enclosed on all sides by something else

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river
emus are large flightless Australian birds
M stands for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Traffic heading north on a motorway beside a river, with birds about in some season.
explanation.walkthrough: The motorway sits inside the birds, the river goes in front, and the whole string REMMUS is then read upwards to give SUMMER.
explanation.definitionFit: Summer is one of the four seasons of the year, so this is a straightforward example relation.

clue.text: Give pardon at Easter? Not entirely

indicators.note: taking a stretch of text but not all of it means the word lies within the run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A question about whether an Easter amnesty should be granted, with a hedging reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking of a royal pardon; the answer is lurking across pardON AT Easter.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to give something, especially money or goods, freely to a cause or person.

clue.text: Upset, maiden goes off in rage

indicators.note: to upset something is to tip it over, so in a down clue the letters are turned upside down

blocks.note: M is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a maiden over
food that goes off decays, or rots

explanation.surface: A distressed young woman flounces out in a fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as an adjective describing the maiden, but it is the instruction to turn MROTS upside down. A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm is to rage, as in storming about the house in a temper; both are verbs of furious behaviour.

clue.text: Was left holding spades

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to exit is to leave, so left is exited
S is the card-playing abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: Someone was abandoned with nothing but spades in their hand at cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was left' reads as one passive verb, but 'Was' is the whole definition and 'left' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Was, in the sense of simply being or having being, is the past of to be, so existed fits.

clue.text: Manipulate The Telegraph's strict nature

blocks.note: to rig an election or a game is to manipulate it
in a Telegraph puzzle the paper's own belongings are ours

explanation.surface: An accusation that the newspaper's famously strict character is being manipulated.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter speaks from inside the paper, so 'The Telegraph's' becomes the possessive 'our'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigour is strictness, severity or exactness, so a strict nature is a fair noun phrase synonym.

clue.text: Came in drunk with an author

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about unsteadily, so the letters stumble into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
W is the standard abbreviation for with
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone staggered in tipsy, arm in arm with a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came in drunk' reads as a complete little story; only the first two words are shuffled, and 'with an' adds the tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan is a celebrated English novelist, author of Atonement and Amsterdam, so he is an example of an author.

clue.text: Lord Chancellor who lost his head supports running church again

blocks.note: a machine that is running is on
CE is the Church of England

blocks.clueFragment: Lord Chancellor who lost his head
blocks.note: Sir Thomas More, Lord Chancellor to Henry VIII, was beheaded in 1535

explanation.surface: A beheaded Lord Chancellor backs a church that is up and running again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost his head' tempts you to drop a first letter, but it simply identifies Thomas More by his execution. In a down clue the piece that supports others sits underneath, so it comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Once more and again both mean one further time, an idiomatic phrase standing in for a single adverb.

clue.text: Press one to alter answer

indicators.note: altering something changes its form, so the letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An automated phone menu: press one to change your reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The phone-menu instruction hides that every letter of 'Press one' is the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A response is a reply or answer given to a question or message, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Instrument Mike and Oscar left at home

blocks.note: Mike is the NATO alphabet word for M
taken as written
Oscar is the NATO alphabet word for O
L is the standard abbreviation for left
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Two men named Mike and Oscar leave a musical instrument behind at the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike and Oscar look like people but are radio-alphabet letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandolin is a small stringed instrument of the lute family, plucked with a plectrum.

clue.text: Bags containing new nibbles

indicators.note: to contain something is to hold it inside, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: sacks are large bags
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Bags of fresh party nibbles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nibbles' could be a verb, but here it is the plural noun for light party food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nibbles is a British word for small savoury snacks such as crisps and nuts served with drinks.

clue.text: Change current from the south

indicators.note: starting at the south end of a down entry means reading it from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a tide is a current of the sea

explanation.surface: Altering an ocean current that flows up from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like an adjective meaning present-day, but it is the noun for a flow of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to change or revise it, so the two verbs are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Reckoned the setter's in property development, primarily

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another
primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: an estate is a piece of landed property
the setter is I, and setter's stands for setter is, giving I'M
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone says the crossword setter has been calculated to be in property development.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves as 'the setter', so 'the setter's' expands to 'I am', shortened to I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: To reckon is to calculate or judge roughly, which is what estimating a figure or amount means.

clue.text: Arrived before ordinary small part

blocks.note: came is the past tense of come, meaning arrived
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

explanation.surface: An actor turns up early for a minor, unremarkable role.
explanation.walkthrough: O for ordinary comes from the old British O levels, the Ordinary level school exams.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a brief appearance by a well-known performer in a film or play, a small role.

clue.text: American editor regularly took drugs

blocks.note: US is the abbreviation for American, as in United States
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A confession that an American newspaper editor had a drug habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like a signal to take alternate letters, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Used, without an object, is slang for habitually taking illegal substances, as in someone who used for years.

clue.text: Briefly read over Rod's card game

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter
in a down clue, one piece over another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: to read a subject at university is to study it
a poker is the metal rod for stirring a fire

explanation.surface: Someone skims through Rod's card game instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name; it is a fire iron, and the 's simply means 'is' joining it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stud poker is a form of poker in which some cards are dealt face up, so it is a type of card game.

clue.text: In the direction of tense scaredy-cats leaving clubs

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so a letter departs from the word

blocks.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
scaredy-cats are cowards
C is the card-playing abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Nervous people walk away from nightclubs in some direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs suggests nightspots, but it is the card suit, giving the C that leaves COWARDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Towards is a preposition meaning heading for or facing, exactly as the phrase describes motion or orientation.

clue.text: Whingers bothered composer

indicators.note: being bothered means being stirred up and disturbed, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Complainers have annoyed a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: A whinger is British slang for a constant complainer. George Gershwin wrote Rhapsody in Blue.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gershwin was an American composer of songs, musicals and concert works, an example of a composer.

clue.text: Morally corrupt – good to take notice

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: decent means good or respectable
an ad, an advertisement, is a notice

explanation.surface: A moral claim that being good means paying attention to corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' reads as a verb meaning observe, but it is a noun, a printed advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent describes moral or cultural decline, self-indulgence and lax standards, which is a corrupt way of living.

clue.text: Perform with partner once, English and sweet

blocks.note: a former partner is an ex
E is the standard abbreviation for English
something sweet and endearing is cute

explanation.surface: Dancing a routine with a former partner who is English and charming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' tempts a dessert, but it is the adjective meaning charming.
explanation.definitionFit: To execute a manoeuvre or plan is to perform or carry it out, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Slippery customers, contemptible people from the East End

indicators.note: London's East End Cockney accent famously drops the H sound at the start of words

blocks.note: a heel is a dishonourable, contemptible person

explanation.surface: Untrustworthy dealers described as low-lifes in Cockney London.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End of London is home to Cockney speech, which drops initial H. 'Slippery customers' sounds like crooks but is literal: the fish are slippery, and jellied eels are an East End dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are long fish with slimy skins, famously hard to grasp, so they are literally slippery creatures.

clue.text: Has that hurt nose occasionally?

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: ow is the cry of someone in pain
the first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone's nose sometimes hurts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That hurt' is read as the exclamation a hurt person makes, not as a description.
explanation.definitionFit: To own something is to have it as your possession, so has and owns are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Seem to follow unfashionable point of view

indicators.note: following something means coming after it, so this piece goes second

blocks.note: something unfashionable is out
to look happy is to seem happy

explanation.surface: Appearing to go along with an opinion that has gone out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seem' comes first in the clue but goes second, because it is told to follow.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlook is a mental attitude or perspective on things, which is what a point of view means.

clue.text: Spot to catch one fish

indicators.note: to catch something is to trap and hold it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a spot is a place or location
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An angler's tip on a good place to land a single fish.
explanation.walkthrough: PLAICE and place sound alike, which gives the clue its neatness.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaice is a flat-bodied European sea fish with orange spots, popular in British fish and chips.

clue.text: I heard politicians in Northern Ireland getting leered at

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by the ear, so the word is chosen for how it is spoken

blocks.note: the pronoun and the organ of sight are pronounced the same
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone hears that Northern Irish politicians have been ogled.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP, the Democratic Unionist Party, is one of Northern Ireland's main political parties.
explanation.definitionFit: To eye someone up is British idiom for looking at them with obvious desire, which is what leering means.

clue.text: Impress representative after son cheers

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it in the answer

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
ta is informal British thanks, like cheers
an MP, a Member of Parliament, is an elected representative

explanation.surface: A parliamentary representative tries to make an impression after a boy toasts him.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers here is the British thank-you, not a toast; ta is its informal equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: To stamp a mark on something is to impress it, pressing a design into a surface.

clue.text: Last-minute recovery from the side

blocks.note: something last-minute is late
a rally is a recovery, as in markets or sport

explanation.surface: A team makes a late comeback, attacking down the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a sports report, but the two words just join to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Laterally means sideways or towards the flank, so it describes movement or approach from the side.

clue.text: Regularly briefing on time in power

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A politician gives regular briefings on their time in office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a joining word but supplies the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A reign is the period during which a monarch rules, a stretch of time holding power.

clue.text: Wife initially helps moose to get molluscs

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife
the opening letter of the word
moose is also plural, and the European word for these deer is elks

explanation.surface: A wife lends a hand to a moose in getting shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: Moose reads as singular, but it is also plural, so it yields ELKS rather than ELK.
explanation.definitionFit: Whelks are edible sea snails, shellfish belonging to the mollusc group, an example relation.

clue.text: Informed guide if it only partially goes the wrong way

indicators.note: taking just part of a run of text means the word lies inside it
going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so the letters read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A satnav-style warning about a guide that sometimes sends you backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in guiDE IF IT ONly, written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To be notified is to be told or given formal notice, so informed is a past participle synonym.

clue.text: Quality of flipping brown river

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: tan is a light brown colour
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Commenting on the character of a muddy brown river, with a mild expletive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word, but it turns TAN around. The Ure is a Yorkshire river much used in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing's nature is its essential character or quality, so the nouns are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Superficial sort boring date with piano

indicators.note: something boring drills into a surface, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a sort is a kind
to date someone is to see them romantically
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: A shallow person is a dull companion at the piano on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' looks like a noun for a type of person, and 'boring' like dull; in fact KIND drills into SEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin-deep describes something only on the surface, like beauty, so it matches superficial as an adjective.
